consensus_summary: Sodom and Gomorrah primarily function as the paradigmatic biblical symbol of extreme human wickedness and sudden, total divine judgment, serving as a standing byword and warning of condemnation across both Testaments; alternatives include sexual immorality, pride/injustice/inhospitality (per Ezekiel), and typological application as a label for apostate covenant cities especially Jerusalem.
book_summary: Sodom and Gomorrah are a spiritual name of Jerusalem, as the prophets address her rulers and people as of Sodom and Gomorrah, Ezekiel identifies Sodom as her sister (with Jerusalem worse), and Revelation applies the name to the city where the Lord was crucified.
consensus_core_identification: paradigm of extreme wickedness and irreversible divine judgment
boundary_disagreement: Book restricts the identification principally to Jerusalem as its spiritual name (via prophetic and apocalyptic application), whereas consensus treats the Jerusalem usage as only one application among broader historical, proverbial, and eschatological cases of extreme wickedness under judgment.
material_contradiction: None; the book does not deny the historical cities, their destruction, or the general symbolism of wickedness and judgment.
rationale: The book's core matches a listed alternative (sometimes minority, sometimes common) in the consensus responses—the typological/prophetic labeling of Jerusalem or corrupt covenant communities—while the settled primary consensus remains the general archetype of wickedness and judgment. The book therefore preserves the overall symbolic category but materially narrows the extension and precision to the Jerusalem case alone, producing a refined boundary rather than equivalence, contradiction, or novelty.
strongest_objection: The consensus primary, grounded in the Genesis narrative plus the bulk of New Testament allusions (Jude, 2 Peter, Jesus' sayings), treats the historical cities as the foundational exemplar of judgment; elevating the secondary Jerusalem application to the core identification subordinates that wider and more settled usage.
